claim: uPAR is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein that promotes tissue remodeling, tumor cell adhesion, migration and invasion.
source: The urokinase receptor (uPAR) is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein that promotes tissue remodeling, tumor cell adhesion, migration and invasion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about uPAR's function.

claim: uPAR mediates degradation of the extracellular matrix through protease recruitment.
source: uPAR mediates degradation of the extracellular matrix through protease recruitment and enhances cell adhesion, migration and signaling through vitronectin binding and interactions with integrins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established mechanism of uPAR function.

claim: uPAR enhances cell adhesion, migration and signaling through vitronectin binding and interactions with integrins.
source: uPAR mediates degradation of the extracellular matrix through protease recruitment and enhances cell adhesion, migration and signaling through vitronectin binding and interactions with integrins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established mechanism of uPAR function.

claim: Full-length uPAR is released from the cell surface.
source: Full-length uPAR is released from the cell surface, but the mechanism and significance of uPAR shedding remain obscure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon.

claim: GDE3 is a GPI-specific phospholipase C that cleaves and releases uPAR.
source: Here we identify transmembrane glycerophosphodiesterase GDE3 as a GPI-specific phospholipase C that cleaves and releases uPAR with consequent loss of function, whereas its homologue GDE2 fails to attack uPAR.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including immunoblotting, LC-MS, and functional assays.

claim: GDE2 fails to attack uPAR.
source: Here we identify transmembrane glycerophosphodiesterase GDE3 as a GPI-specific phospholipase C that cleaves and releases uPAR with consequent loss of function, whereas its homologue GDE2 fails to attack uPAR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis showing no uPAR release in the medium when GDE2 is expressed.

claim: GDE3 overexpression depletes uPAR from distinct basolateral membrane domains in breast cancer cells.
source: GDE3 overexpression depletes uPAR from distinct basolateral membrane domains in breast cancer cells, resulting in a less transformed phenotype, it slows tumor growth in a xenograft model and correlates with prolonged survival in patients.
evidence: This is supported by confocal and super-resolution microscopy data showing reduced uPAR colocalization with GDE3 in membrane domains.

claim: GDE3 overexpression results in a less transformed phenotype in breast cancer cells.
source: GDE3 overexpression depletes uPAR from distinct basolateral membrane domains in breast cancer cells, resulting in a less transformed phenotype, it slows tumor growth in a xenograft model and correlates with prolonged survival in patients.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced cell spreading, lamellipodia formation, colony formation, and matrix degradation.

claim: GDE3 overexpression slows tumor growth in a xenograft model.
source: GDE3 overexpression depletes uPAR from distinct basolateral membrane domains in breast cancer cells, resulting in a less transformed phenotype, it slows tumor growth in a xenograft model and correlates with prolonged survival in patients.
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments showing reduced tumor volume in GDE3-expressing MDA-MB-231 cells compared to controls.

claim: GDE3 expression correlates with prolonged survival in breast cancer patients.
source: GDE3 overexpression depletes uPAR from distinct basolateral membrane domains in breast cancer cells, resulting in a less transformed phenotype, it slows tumor growth in a xenograft model and correlates with prolonged survival in patients.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showing high GDPD2 expression correlates with better survival in triple-negative breast cancer patients.

claim: uPAR is a central player in a complex signaling network implicated in embryo implantation, wound healing and tumor progression.
source: The urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR) is a central player in a complex signaling network implicated in a variety of remodeling processes, both physiological and pathological, ranging from embryo implantation to wound healing and tumor progression (Boonstra et al., 2011; Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: uPAR is a GPI-anchored protein that lacks intrinsic signaling capacity.
source: uPAR is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein and hence lacks intrinsic signaling capacity.
evidence: This is stated as an established property of GPI-anchored proteins.

claim: uPAR acts by binding two major ligands: the protease urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA) and the extracellular matrix protein vitronectin.
source: Instead, uPAR acts by binding two major ligands, namely the protease urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA) and the extracellular matrix (ECM) protein vitronectin (Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Madsen et al., 2007; Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Through uPA binding, uPAR localizes plasmin generation to the cell surface and promotes pericellular proteolysis and ECM degradation.
source: Through uPA binding, uPAR localizes plasmin generation to the cell surface and thereby promotes pericellular proteolysis and ECM degradation (Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Through vitronectin binding and functional interactions with integrins and growth factor receptors, uPAR activates intracellular signaling pathways leading to cytoskeletal reorganization, enhanced cell adhesion and motility.
source: In addition, through vitronectin binding and functional interactions with integrins and growth factor receptors, uPAR activates intracellular signaling pathways leading to cytoskeletal reorganization, enhanced cell adhesion and motility and other features of tissue remodeling and cell transformation (Ferraris et al., 2014; Madsen et al., 2007; Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: uPAR is a master regulator of extracellular proteolysis, cell motility and invasion.
source: As such, uPAR is a master regulator of extracellular proteolysis, cell motility and invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the described functions of uPAR.

claim: uPAR expression is elevated during inflammation and in many human cancers.
source: uPAR expression is elevated during inflammation and in many human cancers, where it often correlates with poor prognosis, supporting the view that tumor cells hijack the uPAR signaling system to enhance malignancy (Boonstra et al., 2011; Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Elevated uPAR expression often correlates with poor prognosis in cancer.
source: uPAR expression is elevated during inflammation and in many human cancers, where it often correlates with poor prognosis, supporting the view that tumor cells hijack the uPAR signaling system to enhance malignancy (Boonstra et al., 2011; Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased uPAR expression in solid tumors and the corresponding activated stroma is being evaluated by PET-imaging for patient stratification.
source: Increased uPAR expression in solid tumors and the corresponding activated stroma is being evaluated by PET-imaging for patient stratification (Persson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Full-length uPAR is released from the plasma membrane resulting in a soluble form (suPAR).
source: It has long been known that full-length uPAR is released from the plasma membrane resulting in a soluble form (suPAR) (Pedersen et al., 1993; Ploug et al., 1992), which is detectable in body fluids and considered a marker of disease severity in cancer and other life-threatening disorders (Haupt et al., 2012; Hayek et al., 2016; Shariat et al., 2007; Sidenius et al., 2000; Stephens et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: suPAR is detectable in body fluids and considered a marker of disease severity in cancer and other life-threatening disorders.
source: It has long been known that full-length uPAR is released from the plasma membrane resulting in a soluble form (suPAR) (Pedersen et al., 1993; Ploug et al., 1992), which is detectable in body fluids and considered a marker of disease severity in cancer and other life-threatening disorders (Haupt et al., 2012; Hayek et al., 2016; Shariat et al., 2007; Sidenius et al., 2000; Stephens et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Circulating suPAR is derived from activated immune and inflammatory cells.
source: Circulating suPAR is derived from activated immune and inflammatory cells (Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Smith and Marshall, 2010), and also from circulating tumor cells (Mustjoki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Circulating suPAR is derived from circulating tumor cells.
source: Circulating suPAR is derived from activated immune and inflammatory cells (Ferraris and Sidenius, 2013; Smith and Marshall, 2010), and also from circulating tumor cells (Mustjoki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Locally produced suPAR might function as a ligand scavenger to confer negative feedback on uPAR.
source: Locally produced suPAR might function as a ligand scavenger to confer negative feedback on uPAR (Smith and Marshall, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both uPAR and suPAR can undergo proteolytic fragmentation by uPA and other proteases, possibly leading to new signaling activities.
source: In addition, both uPAR and suPAR can undergo proteolytic fragmentation by uPA and other proteases, possibly leading to new signaling activities (Montuori and Ragno, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature, with speculation about the functional consequences.

claim: A GPI-specific phospholipase D (GPI-PLD) does not function on native membranes.
source: A GPI-specific phospholipase D (GPI-PLD) (Scallon et al., 1991) has often been assumed to mediate the shedding of GPI-anchored proteins, but this unique PLD does not function on native membranes (Mann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GDE2 promotes neuronal differentiation by cleaving select GPI-anchored proteins, notably a Notch ligand regulator and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (glypicans).
source: A possible clue to the mechanism of uPAR release comes from recent studies showing that a member of the glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase (GDPD/GDE) family (Corda et al., 2014), termed GDE2, promotes neuronal differentiation by cleaving select GPI-anchored proteins, notably a Notch ligand regulator and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (glypicans) (Matas-Rico et al., 2016; Matas-Rico et al., 2017; Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GDE2, GDE3 and GDE6 belong to a GDE subfamily characterized by six-transmembrane-domain proteins with a conserved catalytic ectodomain.
source: GDE2, along with GDE3 and GDE6, belongs to a GDE subfamily characterized by six-transmembrane-domain proteins with a conserved catalytic ectodomain (Figure 1A) (Corda et al., 2009; Matas-Rico et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: GDE3 accelerates osteoblast differentiation through an unidentified mechanism.
source: GDE2's close relative, GDE3, accelerates osteoblast differentiation through an unidentified mechanism (Corda et al., 2009; Yanaka et al., 2003), while the function of GDE6 is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The function of GDE6 is unknown.
source: GDE2's close relative, GDE3, accelerates osteoblast differentiation through an unidentified mechanism (Corda et al., 2009; Yanaka et al., 2003), while the function of GDE6 is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Human GDE2 and GDE3 localized to distinct microdomains at the plasma membrane when expressed at relatively low levels in HEK293 cells.
source: When expressed at relatively low levels in HEK293 cells, human GDE2 and GDE3 (HA-tagged) localized to distinct microdomains at the plasma membrane, possibly representing clustered lipid rafts where GPI-anchored proteins normally reside (Maeda and Kinoshita, 2011), as well as to filopodia-like extensions (Matas-Rico et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: GDE2 and GDE3 localized to filopodia-like extensions in HEK293 cells.
source: When expressed at relatively low levels in HEK293 cells, human GDE2 and GDE3 (HA-tagged) localized to distinct microdomains at the plasma membrane, possibly representing clustered lipid rafts where GPI-anchored proteins normally reside (Maeda and Kinoshita, 2011), as well as to filopodia-like extensions (Matas-Rico et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Human GDE6 was mainly detected in intracellular compartments in HEK293 cells.
source: By contrast, human GDE6 was mainly detected in intracellular compartments and therefore was not further tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: uPAR was readily released into the medium by GDE3 and PI-PLC, but not by GDE2.
source: Strikingly, uPAR was readily released into the medium by GDE3 and PI-PLC, but not by GDE2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 1B showing uPAR in the medium.

claim: GDE3 competed with exogenous PI-PLC to deplete uPAR.
source: GDE3 competed with exogenous PI-PLC to deplete uPAR, since PI-PLC was much less efficient in GDE3-overexpressing than in control HEK-uPAR cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mutating putative active-site residue H229 abolished GDE3 activity without affecting its membrane localization.
source: Mutating putative active-site residue H229, corresponding to H233 in GDE2 (Matas-Rico et al., 2016), abolished GDE3 activity without affecting its membrane localization (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and microscopy data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A transmembrane version of uPAR (uPAR-TM) lacking the GPI moiety was resistant to GDE3 attack.
source: Furthermore, a transmembrane version of uPAR (uPAR-TM) lacking the GPI moiety (Cunningham et al., 2003) was resistant to GDE3 attack, consistent with GDE3 acting through GPI-anchor hydrolysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of GDE3-overexpressing cells confirmed decreased uPAR levels in the plasma membrane.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of GDE3-overexpressing cells confirmed decreased uPAR levels in the plasma membrane (Figure 1D), while TIRF microscopy revealed substantial uPAR loss from the ventral cell surface (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D.

claim: TIRF microscopy revealed substantial uPAR loss from the ventral cell surface in GDE3-overexpressing cells.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of GDE3-overexpressing cells confirmed decreased uPAR levels in the plasma membrane (Figure 1D), while TIRF microscopy revealed substantial uPAR loss from the ventral cell surface (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy data in Figure 1E.

claim: GDE2 and GDE3 have a similar putative GPI-binding groove leading to the active site.
source: While GDE2 and GDE3 have a similar putative GPI-binding groove leading to the active site, they show striking differences in their surface charge distribution, particularly at the putative substrate interaction surface (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on homology modeling shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GDE2 and GDE3 show striking differences in their surface charge distribution, particularly at the putative substrate interaction surface.
source: While GDE2 and GDE3 have a similar putative GPI-binding groove leading to the active site, they show striking differences in their surface charge distribution, particularly at the putative substrate interaction surface (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on homology modeling shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Surface properties are likely a major determinant of selective substrate recognition by GDEs.
source: It therefore seems likely that surface properties are a major determinant of selective substrate recognition by GDEs, a notion that should be validated by future structural studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in surface charge distribution between GDE2 and GDE3.

claim: GDE3-expressing cells failed to shed uPAR from the GDE3-deficient cell population in mixing experiments.
source: By mixing GDE3-expressing cells (lacking uPAR) with uPAR-expressing cells (lacking GDE3), GDE3-expressing cells failed to shed uPAR from the GDE3-deficient cell population (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 2A.

claim: GDE3 acts in cis, attacking uPAR on the same plasma membrane, not on adjacent cells.
source: Thus, GDE3 acts in cis, attacking uPAR on the same plasma membrane, not on adjacent cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the mixing experiment showing no trans activity.

claim: suPAR released by GDE3 did not contain lipid moieties, as shown by Triton X-114 partitioning.
source: Triton X-114 partitioning revealed that suPAR did not contain lipid moieties, as it was not detected in the detergent phase (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Triton X-114 phase separation and immunoblot analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: Acid-treated suPAR samples from GDE3-expressing cells contained inositol 1-phosphate.
source: Subsequent analysis by LC-MS revealed that the acid-treated suPAR samples contained inositol 1-phosphate (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: GDE3 is the first mammalian GPI-specific phospholipase C (GPI-PLC).
source: This result defines GDE3 as the first mammalian GPI-specific phospholipase C (GPI-PLC).
evidence: This is concluded from the LC-MS data showing inositol 1-phosphate, which is the product of phospholipase C cleavage.

claim: HEK-uPAR cells showed markedly increased cell adhesion on vitronectin compared to uPAR-deficient cells.
source: When compared to uPAR-deficient cells, HEK-uPAR cells showed markedly increased cell adhesion, loss of intercellular contacts and enhanced spreading with prominent lamellipodia formation on vitronectin, but not on fibronectin (Figure 3A), typical features of a Rac-driven motile phenotype, in agreement with previous studies (Kjøller and Hall, 2001; Madsen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell adhesion assays in Figure 3A.

claim: HEK-uPAR cells showed loss of intercellular contacts and enhanced spreading with prominent lamellipodia formation on vitronectin, but not on fibronectin.
source: When compared to uPAR-deficient cells, HEK-uPAR cells showed markedly increased cell adhesion, loss of intercellular contacts and enhanced spreading with prominent lamellipodia formation on vitronectin, but not on fibronectin (Figure 3A), typical features of a Rac-driven motile phenotype, in agreement with previous studies (Kjøller and Hall, 2001; Madsen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy images in Figure 3A, 3C, and 3E.

claim: Cell spreading in HEK-uPAR cells on vitronectin coincided with activation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK).
source: Cell spreading coincided with activation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK), indicative of integrin activation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis of FAK phosphorylation in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of GDE3 largely abolished the uPAR-induced phenotypes and cellular responses in HEK-uPAR cells.
source: Strikingly, expression of GDE3 largely abolished the uPAR-induced phenotypes and cellular responses (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple assays shown in Figure 3A-F including adhesion, spreading, lamellipodia formation, and FAK activation.

claim: Catalytically dead GDE3(H229A) had no effect on uPAR-induced phenotypes.
source: Catalytically dead GDE3(H229A) had no effect, neither had overexpressed GDE2 (Figure 3F and results not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell spreading and lamellipodia formation assays in Figure 3F.

claim: By releasing uPAR from the plasma membrane, GDE3 suppresses the vitronectin-dependent activities of uPAR.
source: Thus, by releasing uPAR from the plasma membrane, GDE3 suppresses the vitronectin-dependent activities of uPAR.
evidence: This is concluded from the functional assays showing loss of uPAR activities upon GDE3 expression.

claim: Treatment of diverse cell types with suPAR-enriched conditioned media from HEK293 cells did not evoke detectable cellular responses.
source: Treatment of diverse cell types with suPAR-enriched conditioned media from HEK293 cells did not evoke detectable cellular responses, supporting the notion that suPAR is biologically inactive, at least under cell culture conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: suPAR is biologically inactive, at least under cell culture conditions.
source: Treatment of diverse cell types with suPAR-enriched conditioned media from HEK293 cells did not evoke detectable cellular responses, supporting the notion that suPAR is biologically inactive, at least under cell culture conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cellular responses to suPAR-enriched media.

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells express relatively high levels of uPAR.
source: These cells express relatively high levels of uPAR (Figure 4A) and its ligand uPA (LeBeau et al., 2013), thus forming an autocrine signaling loop.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: MDA-MB-231 cells express uPA, forming an autocrine signaling loop with uPAR.
source: These cells express relatively high levels of uPAR (Figure 4A) and its ligand uPA (LeBeau et al., 2013), thus forming an autocrine signaling loop.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of GDE3 (encoded by GDPD2) is relatively low in breast cancer lines, including MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Expression of GDE3 (encoded by GDPD2) is relatively low in breast cancer lines (n = 51), including MDA-MB-231 cells (Barretina et al., 2012) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis in Figure 4B and supported by a citation.

claim: GDE3 expression in MDA-MB-231 cells led to a modest loss of uPAR from the plasma membrane as shown by flow cytometry.
source: GDE3 expression in MDA-MB-231 cells led to a modest loss of uPAR from the plasma membrane as shown by flow cytometry (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: Basolateral membrane microdomains containing wild-type GDE3 showed little or no colocalization with endogenous uPAR in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Strikingly, basolateral membrane microdomains containing wild-type GDE3 showed little or no colocalization with endogenous uPAR. In marked contrast, catalytically dead GDE3(H229A) clearly colocalized with uPAR in those membrane domains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal and super-resolution microscopy in Figure 4D.

claim: Catalytically dead GDE3(H229A) clearly colocalized with uPAR in basolateral membrane domains in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Strikingly, basolateral membrane microdomains containing wild-type GDE3 showed little or no colocalization with endogenous uPAR. In marked contrast, catalytically dead GDE3(H229A) clearly colocalized with uPAR in those membrane domains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal and super-resolution microscopy in Figure 4D.

claim: Active GDE3 depletes uPAR levels from distinct domains at the basolateral membrane.
source: These results strongly suggest that active GDE3 depletes uPAR levels from distinct domains at the basolateral membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data showing lack of uPAR in GDE3-containing domains.

claim: CRISPR-based knockout of GDE3 resulted in increased basolateral uPAR levels when MDA-MB-231 cells were plated on vitronectin.
source: Consistent with this, CRISPR-based knockout of GDE3 resulted in increased basolateral uPAR levels when the cells were plated on vitronectin (Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy and quantification in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Wild-type MDA-MB-231 cells adopted a motile phenotype on vitronectin, as evidenced by increased cell spreading with marked lamellipodia formation.
source: Wild-type MDA-MB-231 cells adopted a motile phenotype on vitronectin, as evidenced by increased cell spreading with marked lamellipodia formation (Figure 5A–C), strongly reminiscent of a uPAR-regulated phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy and quantification in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Overexpressed GDE3 abolished the vitronectin-dependent phenotype of MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Overexpressed GDE3 abolished the vitronectin-dependent phenotype of MBD-MB-231 cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy and quantification in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Very similar effects of GDE3 overexpression were observed in Hs578T breast cancer cells.
source: Very similar effects of GDE3 overexpression were observed in another uPAR-positive breast cancer cell line (triple-negative Hs578T cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Non-cleavable uPAR-TM largely inhibited the GDE3-induced reduction of cell spreading on vitronectin.
source: To confirm that GDE3 acts through uPAR attack, we expressed non-cleavable uPAR-TM to compete out endogenous uPAR, and found that the GDE3-induced reduction of cell spreading on vitronectin was largely inhibited (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell spreading quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of uPAR gave rise to the same phenotype as GDE3 overexpression, namely reduced cell adhesion, spreading and lamellipodia formation on vitronectin.
source: Furthermore, shRNA-mediated knockdown uPAR (Figure 5D) gave rise to the same phenotype as GDE3 overexpression, namely reduced cell adhesion, spreading and lamellipodia formation on vitronectin (Figure 5E,F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and functional assays in Figure 5D-G.

claim: Wild-type MDA-MB-231 cells showed marked scattering in long-term assays, indicative of increased cell motility with loss of intercellular contacts.
source: In long-term assays, wild-type MDA-MB-231 cells showed marked scattering, indicative of increased cell motility with loss of intercellular contacts (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy and quantification in Figure 6A.

claim: GDE3 overexpression mimicked uPAR depletion in greatly reducing both cell motility and clonogenic potential in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Again, GDE3 overexpression mimicked uPAR depletion either in greatly reducing both cell motility and clonogenic potential, using either shRNA-mediated knockdown (Figure 6A,B) or CRISPR-mediated knockout of uPAR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scattering and colony formation assays in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GDE3 overexpression mimicked uPAR silencing in inhibiting the degradation of a gelatin matrix by MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Also in this cell system, GDE3 overexpression mimicked uPAR silicencing in inhibiting the degradation of a gelatin matrix (mixed with vitronectin) in the presence of serum (Figure 6C,D) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by matrix degradation assays in Figure 6C,D.

claim: GDE3 attenuates the transformed phenotype of uPAR-positive breast cancer cells through loss of functional uPAR.
source: On the basis of these results, we conclude that GDE3 attenuates the transformed phenotype of uPAR-positive breast cancer cells through loss of functional uPAR.
evidence: This is concluded from the multiple functional assays showing GDE3 effects are mediated through uPAR.

claim: GDE3-overexpressing MDA-MB-231 cells showed diminished tumor growth over time in a xenograft model compared to empty vector-expressing cells.
source: When injected into the mammary fat pads of female nude mice, GDE3-overexpressing MDA-MB-231 cells showed diminished tumor growth over time, when compared to empty vector-expressing cells (Figure 7A), consistent with the cell-based data.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor volume measurements in Figure 7A.

claim: High expression of GDPD2 correlates with prolonged relapse-free survival in breast cancer, particularly in triple-negative (basal-like) subtype patients.
source: Finally, in patients, high expression of GDPD2 was found to correlate with prolonged relapse-free survival in breast cancer, particularly in triple-negative (basal-like) subtype patients (N = 618) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: No correlation was found between GDE2 (encoded by GDPD5) expression and survival in breast cancer patients.
source: No such correlation was found for GDE2 (encoded by GDPD5; not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from survival analysis.

claim: GDE3/GDPD2 may serve as a marker of clinical outcome in breast cancer.
source: This suggests that GDE3/GDPD5 may serve as a marker of clinical outcome in breast cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival correlation data.

claim: GPI-anchoring is a complex post-translational modification that anchors select proteins in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: GPI-anchoring is a compIex post-translational modification that anchors select proteins in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Some GPI-anchored proteins are released from their anchor and detected in body fluids.
source: Some GPI-anchored proteins are released from their anchor and detected in body fluids, implying involvement of one or more endogenous GPI-specific hydrolases.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation.

claim: Cleavage and shedding of certain GPI-anchored proteins is mediated by GDE2, thereby promoting neuronal differentiation through multiple signaling pathways.
source: Recent studies have advanced the field by showing that cleavage and shedding of certain GPI-anchored proteins is mediated by a cell-intrinsic transmembrane glycerophosphodiesterase, termed GDE2 (or GDPD5), thereby promoting neuronal differentiation through multiple signaling pathways (Matas-Rico et al., 2016; Matas-Rico et al., 2017; Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GDE3 functions as a GPI-specific PLC that releases uPAR from its anchor.
source: In this study, we focused on the shedding of GPI-anchored uPAR because of its regulatory role in multiple cellular and (patho)physiological activities, while soluble uPAR is considered a biomarker of various human pathologies. Here we report that GDE3 functions as a long-sought GPI-specific PLC that releases uPAR from its anchor.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: As a consequence of GDE3 action, uPAR loses its vitronectin-dependent and matrix-degrading activities in HEK293-uPAR and triple-negative breast cancer cells.
source: As a consequence of GDE3 action, uPAR loses its vitronectin-dependent and matrix-degrading activities, when assayed in HEK293-uPAR and triple-negative breast cancer cells that express both uPAR and uPA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple functional assays.

claim: Loss of uPAR expression by GDE3 was found to be restricted to certain microdomains at the basolateral plasma membrane, where signal transduction is likely to take place.
source: Importantly, loss of uPAR expression by GDE3 was found to be restricted to certain microdomains at the basolateral plasma membrane, where signal transduction is likely to take place.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing localized depletion of uPAR.

claim: By acting as a GPI-specific PLC towards uPAR, GDE3 is a negative regulator of the uPAR signaling network.
source: Thus, by acting as a GPI-specific PLC towards uPAR, GDE3 is a negative regulator of the uPAR signaling network (Figure 7C) that includes uPAR's proteolytic and non-proteolytic activities.
evidence: This is concluded from the functional data showing loss of uPAR activities upon GDE3 expression.

claim: The inhibitory effect of GDE3 overexpression on tumor growth was not dramatic, which is attributed to MDA-MB-231 cells expressing the strongly oncogenic mutant K-RAS protein.
source: Although statistically significant, the inhibitory effect of GDE3 overexpression on tumor growth was not dramatic, which should not come as a surprise since MDA-MBA-31 cells express the strongly oncogenic mutant K-RAS protein, which tends to override the regulation of numerous signaling pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the xenograft data in the context of known oncogenic drivers.

claim: High GDE3 expression correlates with increased survival probability in triple-negative breast cancer patients.
source: Furthermore, high GDE3 expression was found to correlate with increased survival probability in triple-negative breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.

claim: GDE2 overexpression is associated with positive clinical outcome in neuroblastoma patients, which appears attributable to GDE2-induced glypican shedding.
source: Interestingly, our previous work revealed a similar association between overexpression of GDE2 and positive clinical outcome in neuroblastoma patients, which appears attributable to GDE2-induced glypican shedding(Matas-Rico et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GDE3 may cleave additional GPI-anchored substrates whose functional loss could contribute to positive clinical outcome.
source: Furthermore, we cannot rule out that GDE3 may cleave additional GPI-anchored substrates whose functional loss could contribute to positive clinical outcome.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility that cannot be excluded.

claim: Depending on its expression levels, GDE3 may downregulate normal uPAR-dependent remodeling processes.
source: The present results predict that, depending on its expression levels, GDE3 may downregulate normal uPAR-dependent remodeling processes.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: Upregulated GDE3 accelerates osteoblast differentiation in a manner resembling the uPAR knockout phenotype.
source: Indeed, upregulated GDE3 accelerates osteoblast differentiation (Corda et al., 2009; Yanaka et al., 2003) in a manner resembling the uPAR knockout phenotype (Furlan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A striking >200 fold upregulation of GDE3/GDPD2 is observed during blastocyst formation.
source: Furthermore, a striking >200 fold upregulation of GDE3/GDPD2 is observed during blastocyst formation (Munch et al., 2016), implicating GDE3 in the invasion of pre-implantation embryos, a process in which the uPA/uPAR signaling network has been implicated (Multhaupt et al., 1994; Pierleoni et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GDE3 is implicated in the invasion of pre-implantation embryos.
source: Furthermore, a striking >200 fold upregulation of GDE3/GDPD2 is observed during blastocyst formation (Munch et al., 2016), implicating GDE3 in the invasion of pre-implantation embryos, a process in which the uPA/uPAR signaling network has been implicated (Multhaupt et al., 1994; Pierleoni et al., 1998).
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation data and previous knowledge about uPAR in embryo implantation.

claim: GDE3 is upregulated to downregulate uPAR activity in vivo.
source: Although correlative, these results support the view that GDE3 is upregulated to downregulate uPAR activity in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlative data on GDE3 upregulation and uPAR-related phenotypes.

claim: Circulating full-length suPAR should be regarded as a marker of GDE3 activity, not necessarily reflecting uPAR expression levels.
source: The present findings also suggest that circulating full-length suPAR should be regarded as a marker of GDE3 activity, not necessarily reflecting uPAR expression levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that GDE3 releases uPAR.

claim: Homology modeling revealed striking differences in electrostatic surface properties of GDE2 versus GDE3.
source: Homology modeling revealed striking differences in electrostatic surface properties of GDE2 versus GDE3, suggesting that protein-protein interactions may determine substrate recognition by these GDE family members.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Protein-protein interactions may determine substrate recognition by GDE family members.
source: Homology modeling revealed striking differences in electrostatic surface properties of GDE2 versus GDE3, suggesting that protein-protein interactions may determine substrate recognition by these GDE family members.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in surface properties.

claim: Specific GPI-anchor modifications could determine the sensitivity of GPI-anchored proteins to GDE attack.
source: Specific GPI-anchor modifications (Kinoshita and Fujita, 2016; Paulick and Bertozzi, 2008) could also determine the sensitivity of GPI-anchored proteins to GDE attack.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism, supported by citations about GPI modifications.

claim: Vertebrate GDEs, notably GDE2 and GDE3, have evolved to modulate key signaling pathways and alter cell behavior through selective GPI-anchor cleavage.
source: Finally, when regarded in a broader context, the present and previous findings (Matas-Rico et al., 2016; Matas-Rico et al., 2017; Park et al., 2013) support the view that vertebrate GDEs, notably GDE2 and GDE3, have evolved to modulate key signaling pathways and alter cell behavior through selective GPI-anchor cleavage.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion based on the current study and previous work on GDE2.
